questions.question: A hash is one-way: from the hash, you cannot get back the _____.
questions.explanation: The server can only hash a new guess and compare the two hashes; it never needs the original password.

questions.question: Is it true that encrypting passwords with a secret key is as safe as hashing them?
questions.explanation: Encryption can be undone with the key. If an attacker steals the key along with the database, every password is revealed. A hash has no key to steal.

questions.question: What is a salt in password hashing?
options: A secret key the server uses to decrypt passwords
A rule forcing users to pick long passwords
A random value mixed into each password before hashing
A second password the user must remember
questions.explanation: The salt is random per user and stored next to the hash. A is tempting, but a salt is not secret and nothing is ever decrypted.

questions.question: Is it true that two users with the same password get the same Argon2 hash?
questions.explanation: Each user gets a different random salt, so the hashes differ. An attacker can't spot shared passwords or use precomputed tables.

questions.question: Why is a password-hashing algorithm like Argon2 slow on purpose?
questions.answer: So that each guess is expensive: a real user barely notices, but an attacker trying billions of guesses on a stolen hash would need years.
questions.explanation: A fraction of a second doesn't bother a real user who logs in once, but an attacker trying billions of guesses on a stolen hash would need years. Slowness makes brute force too expensive.

questions.question: Why should a login form say "wrong email or password" instead of "no account with this email"?
questions.answer: A precise message reveals which emails have an account (user enumeration), so attackers know which accounts to target.
questions.explanation: A precise message tells an attacker which emails have an account (user enumeration). They can then target those accounts with password guesses or phishing.

questions.question: Why does a server check a dummy hash when the email does not exist?
options: So a wrong email takes as long to answer as a wrong password
To create a new account for that email
To store the wrong password for later analysis
To make the server faster for real users
questions.explanation: Without it, an unknown email would be answered instantly while a known one waits for Argon2, and that time difference would reveal which emails exist. D is wrong: it adds work, it doesn't save any.

questions.question: A JWT has three parts separated by dots: header, payload and _____.
questions.explanation: The signature is computed from the header, the payload and the server's secret, so any change to them breaks it.

questions.question: Is it true that anyone who gets a JWT can read its payload?
questions.explanation: The payload is only base64-encoded, not encrypted. That's why it holds a user id and an expiry, never a password or other secret.

questions.question: What does a valid HS256 signature on a token prove?
options: That the token was made with the server's secret and not changed since
That the user typed the right password just now
That the token can never expire
questions.explanation: Only someone who knows the secret can produce a matching signature. A is the classic mix-up: signing protects against changes, not against reading.

questions.question: The JWT field that says when the token stops being valid is called _____.
questions.explanation: It holds the expiry time. The server rejects tokens past that time, and in the example it also rejects tokens that have no exp at all.

questions.question: Why must a server refuse tokens that use the "none" algorithm?
questions.answer: A "none" token has no signature, so anyone could write any user id in it and log in as that user.
questions.explanation: A "none" token has no signature, so anyone could write any user id in it and log in as that user. The server should accept only the one algorithm it uses, like HS256.

questions.question: Which cookie flag stops JavaScript on the page from reading the token?
questions.explanation: HttpOnly hides the cookie from scripts, so an XSS bug can't steal it. A is tempting, but Secure only controls HTTPS, not who can read it.

questions.question: Is it true that SameSite=Lax stops the browser from sending the cookie on a form POST from another website?
questions.explanation: That blocks CSRF: an evil site can't make your browser submit a logged-in request to the app behind your back.

questions.question: Is it true that the Secure cookie flag encrypts the content of the cookie?
questions.explanation: Secure only means the cookie travels over HTTPS, so nobody on the network sees it. The cookie itself is unchanged.

questions.question: What is the main downside of one long-lived token, and how do refresh tokens help?
questions.answer: A stolen long token works until it expires and can't be cancelled. Refresh tokens keep the access token short-lived and store the long refresh token on the server, where it can be deleted to revoke access.
questions.explanation: A stolen long token works until it expires, and the server can't cancel it. With refresh tokens, the access token lives only minutes, and the long refresh token is stored on the server, where it can be deleted to revoke access.
